newsitem.title: USA: Slow export growth weighs on Asia mkts - Jardine.
newsitem.headline: Slow export growth weighs on Asia mkts - Jardine.

text.p: Slowing export growth due to dropping commodity prices is the main risk faced by investors wanting to put their money into Asian markets, analysts at an investment conference said on Monday.

Participants at the Asia 100 Companies conference organized by Jardine Fleming Securities Ltd said another problem was that many investors had overestimated the rate of return Asian markets could offer.

"The main thing we see this year is a significant slowdown in export growth and the question many investors have been asking is whether this is a cyclical thing or if there are more serious structural problems," N. Ranjan Pal, chief regional economist at Jardine Fleming, said in an interview.
"My conclusion is that they are cyclical," Pal said, adding that they stemmed from a drop in prices of commodities such as steel, petrochemicals and computer chips.

He saw a slow turnaround in the price cycle for computer chips over the next 18 months, a hope bolstered by a steady U.S. book-to-bill ratio that came in at 0.90 in August and is expected to rise to 0.95, according to Wall Street analysts.
Another factor has been the weak performance of Asian markets since they peaked in early 1994, which has shaken the confidence of investors.

"The main problem has been the performance of the markets over the last two-and-a-half to three years because investors have gotten used to the idea that Asian markets are in the vanguard of emerging markets," Jardine Fleming regional strategist Colin Bradbury said in an interview.
"Since the markets peaked in the first quarter of 1994, performance has been relatively disappointing, especially compared to U.S. markets."
This began to change in 1996 and the success of some markets has helped lure investors back.

"The number of markets that are in positive territory this year is probably the biggest since 1993. There are markets which are actually making money this year, which always helps gear up people's enthusiasm," Bradbury said.
He said that, following a dismal showing in July, regional markets have turned around since then to show a solid performance, with Hong Kong, the Philippines and Malaysia coming out on top.

South Korea, Singapore and Sri Lanka were at the bottom with South Korea particularly affected by the drop in chip prices as it specializes in the production of commodity semiconductor chips such as those used in computer memory.
"Korea's export growth has been pulled down significantly because of the decline in computer chip prices," Pal said.
He said the best bet for investors in terms of industry in Asia were telecomms and infrastructure in general, "areas in which Asia has been lacking and is now trying to move ahead."
